200.text:
Governments collect taxes mainly to pay for hospitals, schools, defence and roads, yet they also finance museums, orchestras, festivals and historic buildings, and the question is to what extent tax revenue should be used for cultural projects. I believe that some of it should, but only after essential services are secure.

To begin with, culture deserves a share of public money because it preserves identity and benefits society. Museums, heritage sites and arts education preserve identity and attract tourists. A city that restores its old town and supports a theatre, for example, gains visitors who spend money in hotels and shops, and residents feel pride in their history. Culture also enriches education, since children who learn music, drama or art develop creativity and confidence, and free access to galleries allows poorer families to enjoy it. Private markets alone may not support activities with small audiences, such as classical music or traditional crafts, which would disappear without help.

However, hospitals, schools and housing meet more urgent needs, so culture should receive a limited, accountable share. A government that spends millions on a grand opera house while clinics lack equipment, for example, would be criticised for its priorities. Culture projects should therefore be chosen carefully, with clear aims and regular reports on costs and results. Partnerships with private donors stretch the budget: companies and individuals can sponsor exhibitions, and ticket sales and shops can raise part of the cost. Local communities should also have a say in which projects are funded, so that the money benefits ordinary people and not only an educated minority.

In conclusion, tax revenue should be used for cultural projects to a moderate extent, after essential services have been funded.

202.text:
Many shoppers say that they care about fair wages and the environment, yet few check how products are made, and this essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take to promote ethical consumerism, focusing on reliable information and on incentives.

To begin with, governments can promote ethical consumerism with clear labels, honest reporting and public purchasing. Shoppers need reliable information and incentives, so certified labels, supply-chain disclosure, tax breaks and ethical public procurement make responsible choices easier. A shopper who sees an official label that guarantees fair wages and low emissions, for example, can choose without reading long reports. Companies could be required to publish where their goods come from and under what conditions they are made, and false claims should be punished by fines. Governments are also major buyers of food, uniforms and furniture, so by preferring ethical suppliers, they create a large market and set an example.

In addition, authorities should reward responsible behaviour and educate the public. Lower taxes on certified fair-trade or recycled products make them cheaper than ordinary goods, while higher charges on products that cause serious harm discourage them. Schools can teach pupils about the effects of their purchases, and campaigns can show the real cost of cheap clothing or food. Equally important, governments can support small ethical producers with loans and training so that supply grows to meet demand. Over time, demand for fair and green products rises, which encourages more companies to change their methods.

In conclusion, clear labels, supply-chain transparency, fiscal incentives and education offer the most realistic way to promote ethical consumerism.

205.text:
Every year, large firms announce that they will merge with rivals, and opinions differ on whether corporate mergers are good for the economy. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that mergers create efficient, innovative firms. Larger companies share costs, invest in research and compete abroad. Two pharmaceutical firms that merge, for example, can combine laboratories and sales networks, develop new medicines faster and reach more countries. Duplicate offices and factories can be closed, which lowers prices or raises profits, and bigger firms may find it easier to raise money for large projects. In industries that need huge investment, such as airlines or telecommunications, small companies may be unable to survive, so mergers can save businesses and jobs. National champions can also compete with giant foreign rivals.

On the other hand, critics argue that mergers may reduce competition and jobs. Fewer rivals can mean higher prices, less choice and redundancies. A merger between the two biggest supermarkets in a region, for example, may leave customers with little choice and give the new company power over suppliers, who must accept low prices. Staff may lose their jobs when departments are combined, and small competitors may be driven out. Large firms can also become complacent and slow to innovate when they face little competition. Competition authorities should approve only beneficial deals. They can require firms to sell some operations, set conditions on prices and service, or block mergers that would create a dominant position.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that mergers can benefit the economy when they increase efficiency and innovation, but regulators must prevent deals that harm competition.

218.text:
Some people put aside part of every salary, while others enjoy their money as they earn it, and opinions differ on whether it is better to save or to spend freely. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of saving argue that it brings security. Savers can meet emergencies and long-term goals. A family with several months of income in the bank, for example, can survive the loss of a job or an unexpected hospital bill without borrowing, and they can pay a deposit on a home or finance their children's education. Saving encourages discipline and reduces stress, because people feel more in control of their future. In old age, savings supplement a pension. Money that is saved and invested also provides funds for businesses to grow, so that it benefits the wider economy.

On the other hand, supporters of spending argue that life should be enjoyed now and that spending supports the economy. Those who never spend miss experiences, and nobody can be sure that they will live to enjoy their savings. A young couple who use their money to travel together, for example, create memories that last for life. Spending also supports shops, restaurants and jobs, and when consumers cut back too much, the economy slows. However, heavy spenders risk debt, and a sudden loss of income can lead to serious difficulty. A budget with both is most sensible. Many financial advisers suggest using a fixed share of income for needs, for wants and for saving, which allows people to enjoy the present while preparing for the future.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that a balance between saving and spending is wisest, with enough saving to be secure and enough spending to enjoy life.

Hưởng hiện tại, hỗ trợ kinh tế: không chi bỏ lỡ trải nghiệm, không chắc sống để hưởng; ví dụ cặp trẻ du lịch tạo ký ức cả đời; chi tiêu nuôi cửa hàng, nhà hàng, việc làm; cắt quá nhiều kinh tế chậm; nhưng chi nhiều nợ, mất thu nhập đột ngột khó khăn; ngân sách cả hai: tỷ lệ cố định cho nhu cầu, mong muốn, tiết kiệm.

225.text:
Ships, planes and cables carry goods, services and money between almost every country, and opinions differ on whether global trade benefits all countries. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that global trade benefits countries on average. Specialisation and larger markets raise efficiency and lower prices. A country with a warm climate that exports fruit and imports machinery, for example, can enjoy goods that it could produce only at a very high cost, and its farmers sell to millions of customers abroad. Trade brings competition, which encourages firms to improve quality and to innovate, and it gives consumers cheaper and more varied products. Many countries in East Asia grew rapidly by exporting manufactured goods and lifted millions of people out of poverty. Trade also creates links between nations that make conflict less likely.

On the other hand, critics argue that gains are uneven and some countries lose. Poorer countries may rely on raw exports with unstable prices, while the profits of processing go elsewhere. Industries that cannot compete close, workers lose their jobs and communities decline. A country that depends on selling a single crop, for example, may suffer badly when its price falls on world markets. Unequal bargaining power allows rich countries to set rules in their favour, and trade can encourage pollution and poor working conditions. Fair rules and support for losers are needed. These include trade agreements that protect labour and environmental standards, aid for developing nations to build industries and retraining for displaced workers.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that global trade benefits most countries over time, but it does not benefit all equally, so cooperation and fair rules are essential.

233.text:
Machines that build objects layer by layer from plastic, metal or even concrete are already used in hospitals, factories and homes, and the question is how far 3D printing will change manufacturing within twenty years. I believe that it will transform some areas greatly, although it will not replace mass production.

To begin with, 3D printing will transform prototypes, custom parts and spare supplies. It makes complex or personalised items quickly and cuts waste and transport. An engineer who wants to test a new design, for example, can print a model overnight instead of waiting weeks for a factory to make a mould. Dentists already print crowns and hearing-aid shells that fit each patient exactly, and surgeons use printed models to plan operations. Remote places such as ships, mines and space stations can print spare parts on the spot rather than carry large stocks. Because the printer adds material rather than cutting it away, less is wasted, and products can be designed in shapes that were once impossible.

However, 3D printing is slow and costly for large production runs and limited in materials. A car manufacturer that needs a million identical door handles, for example, can make them far more cheaply by casting or stamping. Printed objects are often weaker or rougher than those made by traditional methods, and only a limited range of plastics and metals can be used. Quality control and intellectual property also raise problems, since anyone with a file can copy a product. It will complement factories rather than replace them. In twenty years, printers will be common in workshops, hospitals and some homes, but most everyday goods will still come from conventional factories.

In conclusion, 3D printing will change manufacturing to a considerable extent in certain areas, but it will not replace mass production.

243.text:
Billboards, television adverts and online banners surround us, and this essay will discuss the role of advertising in shaping consumer culture, focusing on the creation of wants and on its social effects.

To begin with, advertising shapes consumer culture by creating wants and defining what is fashionable. Constant messages link products to identity and success, so people buy for status. A teenager who sees a sports shoe worn by a famous player in every advertisement, for example, may feel that he needs it in order to fit in, although his old shoes still work. Advertisers use emotion, humour and attractive images to make goods appear exciting, and new models are presented as essential every year. Seasonal campaigns such as sales and gift seasons teach people to spend at certain times. Over time, this builds a culture in which shopping is a leisure activity and possessions measure personal worth.

However, advertising also has useful functions. It informs buyers about new products, prices and choices, and it makes competition between companies possible, which can lower prices. Advertising revenue pays for much of the media, from free websites to television channels. Some campaigns promote health, safety or charity, and can influence behaviour in positive ways. Consumers need critical awareness. Schools can teach young people to recognise persuasion techniques, regulators can ban misleading claims and limit advertising to children, and individuals can ask themselves whether they really need a product before buying it.

In conclusion, advertising plays a major role in shaping consumer culture by creating wants and setting social standards, although it also informs and funds the media.

278.text:
Some shoppers pay with banknotes and coins, while others tap a card or a phone, and opinions differ on whether cash or digital payments are better. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of cash argue that it offers privacy and control. Notes work without power and make spending visible. A person who takes a fixed amount of cash to the market each week, for example, can see exactly how much is left and is less likely to overspend. Cash leaves no digital record, which protects privacy, and it can be used by people without bank accounts, such as children, tourists and the elderly. During power cuts or system failures, cash is often the only way to buy essentials. It also avoids card fees, which small traders must pay for every transaction.

On the other hand, supporters of digital payments argue that they offer speed and records. Cards and apps are faster, safer from theft and easier to track, but they depend on technology. A traveller who pays by phone abroad, for example, avoids carrying large sums and exchanging currency, and a shop assistant does not have to count change. Digital payments produce statements that help people to budget and make it harder to evade tax. They also allow online shopping and instant transfers to friends and family. However, cyberattacks, outages and the risk of overspending are drawbacks. Having both options is practical. People can use digital payments for convenience and keep some cash for emergencies and for situations where privacy or reliability matter.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I prefer digital payments for everyday use, but I believe that cash should remain widely accepted.

316.text:
Parcels arrive within hours, and vans from large platforms are seen in every street, so many people think that fast delivery services harm local businesses. I agree to some extent, since large platforms attract customers away from small shops, although the same services can help independent sellers.

To begin with, fast delivery services favour large platforms. Big companies with warehouses and low prices attract shoppers away from local shops. A bookshop that sells a novel for the full price, for example, loses a customer who can order it online at a discount and receive it the next morning. Large platforms can afford loss-making offers, free delivery and returns, which small shops cannot match. As more people expect speed and convenience, high-street shops lose footfall, and many have closed, leaving empty units and reducing local employment. Money spent on the platform often leaves the community, while a local shop keeps wages and profits in the area.

However, independent businesses can use the same networks to sell more widely. A small craft maker who lists products on a marketplace and uses a courier, for example, can reach customers hundreds of kilometres away, who would never have found her shop. Local restaurants, florists and bakeries use delivery apps to attract new clients, and many shops have launched their own websites. Local firms must adapt and offer service that platforms cannot. They can provide expert advice, personal attention, unique products and fast local delivery by their own staff, and they can emphasise community links. Councils can support them by reducing business charges and improving parking and the appearance of town centres.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that fast delivery services harm local businesses, but those that adapt can benefit from them.

319.text:
Some governments encourage factories to pay fair wages, protect workers and limit pollution, and this essay will discuss the benefits for a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing, using examples such as Germany and Bangladesh.

To begin with, a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing gains reputation, skilled workers and sustainable growth. Fair wages and clean production attract responsible buyers, reduce accidents and pollution costs and build trust in exports. Germany, for example, is known for high-quality products made under strict safety and environmental rules, and many consumers are willing to pay more for goods marked "made in Germany". After a deadly factory collapse in 2013, Bangladesh introduced safety inspections and fire standards, which restored the confidence of international clothing brands. Healthy and well-paid workers are more productive and less likely to leave, so firms save on training and recruitment, and fewer accidents mean lower costs.

Furthermore, ethical manufacturing protects the environment and the community. Factories that treat waste water and reduce emissions avoid fines, cleanup costs and damage to local health and farming. Workers who earn enough support their families and spend in local markets, which stimulates the domestic economy. Companies that follow high standards find it easier to enter foreign markets with strict import rules, and investors increasingly prefer responsible firms. The main disadvantage is the higher initial cost of safer equipment and better wages, but long-term competitiveness rises as quality and reputation improve. A country can support its producers with training, loans for cleaner technology and clear, consistently enforced regulations.

In conclusion, a country that focuses on ethical manufacturing benefits through reputation, productivity, environmental protection and long-term competitiveness, despite higher initial costs.

Danh tiếng, lao động có kỹ năng, tăng trưởng bền: lương công bằng, sản xuất sạch thu hút người mua có trách nhiệm, giảm tai nạn, chi phí ô nhiễm, tin cậy xuất khẩu; ví dụ Đức nổi tiếng sản phẩm chất lượng cao theo quy tắc an toàn, môi trường nghiêm, nhiều người sẵn trả hơn cho hàng 'made in Germany'; sau vụ sập nhà máy 2013 Bangladesh kiểm tra an toàn, tiêu chuẩn cháy khôi phục niềm tin của hãng quần áo quốc tế; công nhân khoẻ, lương tốt năng suất, ít nghỉ.

Bảo vệ môi trường, cộng đồng: xử lý nước thải, giảm khí thải tránh phạt, dọn dẹp, hại sức khoẻ, nông nghiệp; lao động đủ sống chi tiêu địa phương kích thích kinh tế; dễ vào thị trường nước ngoài quy tắc nghiêm; nhà đầu tư thích; nhược: chi phí ban đầu thiết bị an toàn, lương; cạnh tranh dài hạn; đào tạo, vay công nghệ sạch, quy định rõ.
Danh tiếng, năng suất, môi trường, cạnh tranh dài hạn dù chi phí ban đầu cao.
